opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the first thing I'd do is resist the urge to immediately write my own controller and put it on the hardware. Most of these robots come with a default locomotion controller, so I'd start there: get it walking, see how it behaves, get a feel for the hardware, how the motors respond, what the latency looks like, how robust it is when you push it a bit. That gives you a baseline for everything that follows.

Then, before touching anything on the real robot, I'd set up a good simulation of it. For me that's really the core of the workflow. You want an accurate model: the URDF, the masses, the joint limits, and especially the actuator dynamics, because that's usually where the sim-to-real gap bites you. With a massively parallel simulator on a single GPU you can train thousands of robots at once, so you can get a walking policy with reinforcement learning in minutes rather than days. That fast iteration loop is what makes experimenting fun and productive.

Once you have a policy in sim, you add the things that make it transfer: domain randomization on friction, mass, motor strength, some noise on observations, random pushes, a terrain curriculum so it learns to handle rough ground and stairs gradually. Then I'd test it carefully on the real robot: start with it suspended or on a harness, low gains, a safety stop ready, and only then let it walk on flat ground before going to harder terrain.

And from there it's an iterative loop. You see where it fails on the real robot, you figure out whether that's a modeling issue or a missing randomization, go back to simulation, fix it, retrain, and deploy again. The nice thing is that loop is now fast enough that you can really explore, try new behaviors, new terrains, even things like jumping or climbing, without being afraid of breaking the hardware every time.

r001.rationale: The response recommends starting with the robot’s default locomotion controller and building experiments around it. It does not identify rebuilding the existing software stack from scratch as a central challenge.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the first thing I'd say is that, honestly, the robot out of the box is already quite capable. Something like a Spot or a Unitree comes with a controller that walks fine on flat ground, and you can just drive it around with a joystick for a while and get a feel for what the hardware can do, how it reacts when you push it, where it starts to struggle. I think that's actually an important step, because it builds intuition for the physical system before you try to replace anything.

But of course, the interesting part for us is when you want to put your own controller on it. And there I wouldn't start by training a policy and deploying it on day one. I'd start with the simulation. You need a good model of the robot, the URDF, the actuator properties, and you need to check that the simulated robot actually behaves like the real one. A lot of the sim-to-real gap is just mismatch in things like motor response, latency, friction in the joints, and it's worth spending time there up front, because every policy you train later inherits those errors.

Then, once you have a simulation you trust, that's where we train with reinforcement learning. With GPU-based simulation we can run thousands of robots in parallel, so training a walking policy takes minutes rather than days, and that changes how you experiment. You can try a reward formulation, see it fail, change it, and iterate many times in a day. I'd also use domain randomization quite aggressively, randomizing masses, friction, pushing the robot around in simulation, so that the policy is robust by the time you transfer it.

And then on the real robot, I'd go step by step. First just verify the low-level interface, send small commands, check joint directions and gains. Then run the policy on a stand, with the legs in the air, to see that it reacts sensibly. Then on the ground with someone ready to catch it, or with a harness. It sounds overly careful, but a robot falling badly can break something, and that costs you a lot more time than being patient.

The last thing I'd say is to push it into situations where it fails. Flat ground is easy. Stairs, slippery surfaces, getting kicked, those are where you learn what's actually missing, and that's what guides the next round of experiments in simulation. It's really a loop between the two.

r001.rationale: The response describes replacing the robot’s controller and developing a policy through simulation and real-world testing, but does not identify rebuilding the existing software stack from scratch as a central challenge.

astra-6.text:
I would start with a very simple experiment, just to understand how the robot behaves. Before trying to make it walk, I’d check the joint commands, the sensor readings, and the safety mechanisms. With the robot supported, you can move one joint at a time and make sure everything behaves as you expect.

Then I’d move to standing and taking a few slow steps. If the goal is to learn a locomotion policy, I’d do most of that experimentation in simulation first. You can try things much faster there, and falling over is much less expensive. Once you have something that works, you transfer it to the real robot carefully and look at where its behavior differs from the simulation. Those differences tell you what to improve next.

r001.rationale: The response recommends checking commands, sensors, and safety mechanisms, then experimenting with steps and simulation. It does not identify rebuilding the robot’s existing software stack from scratch as a central challenge.

sol-6.1.text:
I would start with whatever controller comes with the robot, just to get a feel for how it behaves. Can it stand up reliably? How does it walk? What happens when you give it different commands? You want to understand the hardware and the interface before trying anything too ambitious.

Then I’d move into simulation. That gives you a place to experiment with a controller, let it fall over, and try again without damaging the robot. Once you have something that works reasonably well there, you can transfer it to the real system and start carefully—small motions, low speeds, and a way to stop it quickly. The interesting part is seeing where the real robot behaves differently from the simulation and using that to improve the next experiment.

r001.rationale: The response recommends trying the supplied controller and then experimenting in simulation, but does not identify rebuilding the robot’s existing software stack from scratch as a central challenge.
